title: Balanitis: soreness of the penis head and getting the cause checked
intro: Balanitis means inflammation of the glans, the head of the penis. The foreskin may also be inflamed. Soreness, itching, swelling or discharge can have several causes, including irritation, infection or a skin condition. It is not automatically a sexually transmitted infection or a sign of poor hygiene. Treatment works best when it addresses the cause, while severe swelling or trouble passing urine needs prompt help.

sections.heading: Describe the changes and possible irritants
paragraphs: Explain when symptoms started, whether they recur and whether there is pain with urination, discharge, bleeding or a rash elsewhere. Redness may be less obvious on darker skin, so tenderness and swelling also matter. Mention new soaps, lubricants, condoms, washing products and medicines, as well as relevant sexual exposure. Harsh or excessive washing can aggravate delicate skin. Do not assume every sore penis needs an antifungal cream or that a familiar symptom proves the same cause as last time.

sections.heading: Allow an assessment that distinguishes different causes
paragraphs: A clinician may examine the skin and consider a swab or other tests according to the findings. Testing for sexually transmitted infections may be appropriate with relevant symptoms or exposure. Recurrent or troublesome episodes may prompt checks for diabetes or another contributing condition. You can request privacy, an interpreter or a chaperone and ask what an examination involves. A persistent sore, ulcer, lump or unexplained bleeding needs reassessment rather than repeated unconfirmed treatment, because other skin diseases and less common serious causes must be considered.

sections.heading: Use gentle care without forcing the foreskin
paragraphs: Clean gently with lukewarm water and dry carefully; avoid fragranced products, harsh disinfectants and scrubbing. In adults, retract only if it moves comfortably and return the foreskin to its usual position afterwards. Never force back a child's foreskin that is still attached or tight. During painful inflammation, ask the clinician how to clean safely rather than repeatedly manipulating it. Do not insert objects or use home-made chemical treatments. If a particular product appears to irritate, stop using it and discuss a suitable alternative.

sections.heading: Match prescribed treatment to the diagnosis
paragraphs: Depending on the cause, treatment may involve an antifungal, an antibiotic or an anti-inflammatory cream selected by the clinician. These medicines are not interchangeable. Confirm where to apply a prescribed product, how long to use it and when to return if it fails. Ask about sex, partner testing and whether a cream affects condom reliability when relevant. Repeated episodes or a problematic tight foreskin may justify specialist advice; surgery is considered in selected cases, rather than being inevitable after one episode. Avoid using someone else's cream or prolonging treatment yourself.

sections.heading: Recognise symptoms that cannot wait for a routine visit
paragraphs: Inability to pass urine requires urgent medical help. A foreskin stuck behind the glans with increasing swelling or pain is an emergency: do not wait for it to settle or repeatedly force it. Severe pain, rapidly spreading swelling, fever or feeling unwell also needs urgent assessment. If treatment has not helped, symptoms return or a skin change remains, arrange a review even if discomfort is mild. Early reassessment can prevent repeated treatment of the wrong cause and clarify whether further investigation is needed.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: symptoms after a new product
examples.text: An adult develops soreness after changing shower products. They stop the fragranced product, clean gently and seek assessment when symptoms persist. They describe the timing and any sexual exposure rather than assuming irritation rules out every other cause.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: a child with painful swelling
examples.text: A child has a sore swollen foreskin. Their carer does not force it back to clean underneath. They arrange assessment and explain whether the child can pass urine; inability to urinate would require urgent help.

questions: Which cause best fits the findings, and would a swab, infection testing or diabetes check help?
How should I clean the area and use the prescribed treatment, and what should I avoid?
